title: Model-based RL and Planning
oneLiner: If you can predict how the world will respond, you can think ahead: practise in your head between real moves (Dyna) or search through possible futures before choosing (tree search).

what.html:
Model-based RL learns or is given a model: a way to predict what happens after an action. The agent can then plan, improving its decisions using imagined experience instead of only real experience. Dyna-Q replays remembered moves in its head between real steps; Monte Carlo tree search explores possible futures from the current position before each move. Systems like AlphaGo combine tree search with learned networks.

Everyday versionA chess player imagines "if I move here, they'll probably reply there…" before touching a piece; a driver who learned the city's layout can work out a detour without trying every street.

why.html:
• Real experience is often expensive; imagined experience is cheap.
  • Search + learning produced superhuman Go, chess and shogi players.
  • Learned world models let robots and agents train "in imagination".

how.title: What is a model?
how.html: Anything that predicts the next state and reward. A full probability table (what dynamic programming needs) or just a simulator that gives one possible outcome per call.

how.title: Dyna: practise in your head
how.html: After each real step: learn from it, remember what happened, then replay n remembered moves to update values again. In a small maze, 50 imagined updates per real step cut the second episode from about 600 steps to about 45.

how.title: When the world changes
how.html: A remembered model can go out of date (a new shortcut opens). Dyna-Q+ gives a small bonus to moves not tried for a long time, so the agent goes back and checks.

how.title: Choosing which branch to explore
how.html: In a search tree, score each branch by its win rate plus a bonus for being rarely tried. A branch tried 2 times out of 100 gets a much bigger bonus (2.74) than one tried 10 times (1.557) with the same win rate.

how.title: Monte Carlo tree search
how.html: Repeat: walk down the tree choosing promising branches, add a new position, play it out quickly to the end, and send the result back up. Then play the most-explored move.

how.title: AlphaGo and friends
how.html: Neural networks suggest good moves and judge positions, so the search wastes less time. AlphaGo Zero learned without human games; MuZero even learned the rules itself.

how.title: Learned world models
how.html: An agent can learn a model of the world from pixels and practise inside it. But small prediction errors add up over long imagined sequences, and planners love to exploit model mistakes.

demo.html: Run episodes in the maze with 0, 5 or 50 planning steps. With planning, the shading (learned value) spreads back from the goal almost immediately and the path shortens after just a couple of episodes.

example.html:
Why planning helps so much. In the first episode the agent wanders until it stumbles on the goal; only the very last move learns anything. Without planning, the value creeps back one state per episode. With Dyna-Q, every imagined replay of remembered moves can pass that value one step further back, so dozens of states learn before the next real step.

Supplementary Tree search is only as good as its evaluations: from 21 sticks in Nim, random playouts barely tell the moves apart, which is why AlphaGo replaced them with a learned value network.

misunderstandings: Planning requires a perfect probability model.
A sample model (simulator, remembered transitions) is enough.
Model errors can mislead the planner.
UCB focuses simulations on promising and uncertain branches.
takeaways: Models predict transitions; planning improves policies from simulated experience.
Dyna-Q = direct RL + model learning + n planning updates per step.
Dyna-Q+ adds κ√τ to revisit stale transitions.
MCTS: selection (UCB1), expansion, simulation, backup; worked UCB 1.557 vs 2.74.
AlphaGo → AlphaZero → MuZero; world models face model bias.
thirty: Model-based RL uses distribution models (full p(s′, r|s, a)) or sample models (simulators, learned transitions) to plan, i.e. to improve a policy from simulated experience. Dyna-Q combines direct Q-learning, model learning and n planning updates per real step; in a maze, 50 planning steps cut episode 2 from about 605 to about 45 steps. Dyna-Q+ adds an exploration bonus κ√τ for long-untried transitions to cope with changing environments. MCTS performs decision-time planning by selection with UCB1 (Q + c√(ln N/n): 1.557 for n = 10, 2.74 for n = 2 at N = 100), expansion, rollout simulation and backup. AlphaGo combined policy/value networks with MCTS; AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero learned by self-play alone; MuZero learns its own latent model. World models (PlaNet, Dreamer) enable training in imagination, but compounding errors and model bias require short rollouts, ensembles and real-data correction.
